title: Proofing bread dough
subtitle: understanding and managing the final rise before baking
excerpt: Proofing is the final rise of shaped bread dough before it goes into the oven. The yeast produces carbon dioxide, which inflates the gluten structure built during kneading. The dough is ready to bake when it has roughly doubled in size and a finger poked into the surface leaves an indent that springs back slowly. Under-proofed bread is dense; over-proofed bread collapses in the oven.
sourceNotes: Bread proofing guidance documented in British baking manuals from at least the eighteenth century. Method consistent across standard British bread-baking instruction.

glossaryTerms.definition: The first rise of bread dough, before shaping, when the yeast ferments the sugars in the flour and begins building flavour and gas. Distinct from the final proof which happens after shaping.
The second and final rise of shaped bread dough before it goes into the oven. The dough inflates as the yeast produces carbon dioxide into the gluten structure.

content.text: happens after the dough has been shaped and placed in its tin or on its tray. It differs from the
in two ways: the dough is in its final shape, and the focus is on inflation rather than flavour development. The time it takes varies with temperature, yeast quantity, and dough hydration.

A warm, draught-free spot at around 24 to 26°C gives the fastest proof. A cooler room (18°C) will take twice as long. The fridge (4°C) gives an overnight cold proof, which is slower and develops more flavour. There is no fixed time: you are looking for a specific size and feel, not a clock.
Flour a finger and press it about 1 cm into the surface of the dough. Watch the indent:
If the indent springs back immediately and completely: the dough is under-proofed. Continue proofing.
If the indent springs back slowly and partially: the dough is ready to bake.
If the indent does not spring back and the surface looks wrinkled or deflated: the dough is over-proofed. Bake immediately; it may still be edible but the crumb will be denser.

Shaped dough can be placed in a lightly oiled, covered bowl or tin in the fridge for 8 to 16 hours for a cold proof. The slow fermentation develops more complex flavour. Take the dough out of the fridge about 30 minutes before baking and check the poke test before loading into the oven.

attrs.avoid: Avoid a draught or cold area; yeast becomes sluggish below 18°C.
attrs.fix: Move to a warmer spot (near a warm oven, or inside the oven with just the light on) and wait. If after 3 hours there is no visible rise, the yeast may have been killed; check the yeast freshness.

attrs.problem: Dough collapses when scored before baking
attrs.avoid: Avoid over-proofing; once the gluten is over-stretched it cannot hold the gas and will deflate on any disturbance.
attrs.fix: Bake immediately without scoring if the dough collapses. It will still bake but the crust will crack unpredictably.

attrs.problem: Crust skin forming on the dough surface during proofing
attrs.avoid: Avoid leaving the dough uncovered in a warm room; the surface dries out quickly.
attrs.fix: Cover the dough with lightly oiled cling film or a damp tea towel during the proof.
